subject: The fitted-bedroom journey from measure to installation
hook: No bedroom wall is straight. This strip deals with it.
ig:
No bedroom wall is straight. This strip deals with it.

It is called a scribed filler, and it is one of the reasons we measure so carefully at the survey stage.

Older Staffordshire houses especially have walls that lean, bow or wander by the time they reach the ceiling. If a wardrobe was pushed straight against that wall you would see a tapering gap, or the doors would be forced out of square to close it.

Instead, we plan a filler panel at the end of the run. On fitting day it is marked to the wall's exact line and trimmed to match, so the cabinets stay level and square and the wall-side edge looks built in.

The same idea applies at the ceiling, where a top filler takes up any dips.

Which detail bothers you most in your bedroom: gaps, dust tops or uneven doors? Tell us in the comments.
fb:
Here's a small detail that makes a big difference to how a fitted wardrobe looks.

Most of the bedroom walls we survey around Stoke-on-Trent aren't perfectly straight, and older houses can be well out. Rather than leave a gap down the side, we fit a scribed filler: a panel cut on site to follow the exact line of your wall. The cabinets stay level, the doors hang true, and it looks like it grew there.
